```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_desolve <- requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)
```

This vignette is the honest inventory: what `r2sbml` does not do, what it does
only partially, and — the part that matters most in practice — **which of those
gaps announce themselves and which do not**.

Read `vignette("r2sbml", package = "r2sbml")` first for how the package is meant
to be used.

```{r library}
library(r2sbml)
ex <- function(f) system.file("examples", f, package = "r2sbml")

# convertReactions() reports progress on the console; keep only the warnings
convert <- function(file, format = "R", out = tempfile()) {
  tryCatch({
    invisible(capture.output(convertReactions(file, out, format = format)))
    cat("no warning\n")
  }, warning = function(w) cat(conditionMessage(w), "\n"))
  invisible(out)
}
sbml_file <- function(body) {
  f <- tempfile(fileext = ".xml")
  writeLines(sprintf('<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<sbml xmlns="http://www.sbml.org/sbml/level3/version2/core" level="3" version="2">
<model>%s</model>
</sbml>', body), f)
  f
}
```

# The single most important table

Generated code that fails loudly is a nuisance. Generated code that runs and
quietly returns the wrong numbers is a hazard. Here is where each limitation
falls:

| Limitation | How you find out |
| --- | --- |
| Coupled or nonlinear algebraic rules in mrgsolve / rxode2 / ubiquity | **R warning** + comment in the file |
| Coupled or nonlinear algebraic rules that do not form a square system | **R warning** + comment |
| Dilution for an assignment-rule volume that cannot be differentiated | **R warning** |
| A value the model leaves undefined | **R warning**, written as `NaN` |
| Constructs with no ubiquity spelling | **R warning** + `# WARNING` block in the file |
| An id renamed because the target reserves it | console message |
| `delay` in the other five targets | **silent** — code fails at run time |
| `root(n, x)` of a negative `x`, `n` not a literal | **silent** — `NaN`, even for an odd `n` |
| Events | **silent** — a count in the header comment only |
| `factorial` in C++ and Julia | **silent** — untested |
| Inconsistent initial conditions for a DAE | solver error, not mentioning SBML |
| A semantically invalid model | **silent** — nothing is validated |

Everything below expands on these.

# How far the output has been checked

The deSolve output is checked numerically against the
[SBML Test Suite](https://github.com/sbmlteam/sbml-test-suite): each case is
converted, simulated and compared with the suite's expected time course within
the case's own tolerances. Of the 1011 semantic cases in scope, **1007 pass**.
"In scope" leaves out every case using a construct `r2sbml` does not translate:
events, `delay`, `rateOf`, fast reactions, `stoichiometryMath` and the SBML
Level 3 packages. The four that fail in scope are listed at the end.

The other five targets share the same model preparation and the same
expression rewriting, so most of what the suite checks applies to them too —
but they are verified only on purpose-built probe models, against closed-form
solutions: mrgsolve and rxode2 compiled and run, MATLAB under Octave, Julia
with `DifferentialEquations.jl`, and ubiquity by reading the generated system
file. None of them is run against the full suite.

# Scope: reading and exporting only

`r2sbml` has no setter API. You cannot change a species' initial value, add a
reaction, or write SBML back out. There is no `setSpecies()`, no
`writeSBML()`, and `getModel()` returns an opaque external pointer rather than
an R-side object you could edit.

If you need to modify models programmatically, use libSBML's own R bindings or
edit the XML directly. `r2sbml` is for inspecting a model and getting simulation
code out of it.

# Per-target capability matrix

| Feature | deSolve | mrgsolve | rxode2 | MATLAB | Julia | ubiquity |
| --- | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| Rate rules / reactions | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Assignment rules, returned as outputs | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Boundary / constant species | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Initial-condition unit conversion | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Algebraic rules linear in one unknown | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Coupled or nonlinear algebraic rules (DAE) | yes | no | no | yes | yes | no |
| Compartment with a rate rule, and dilution | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Compartment with an assignment rule, and dilution | mostly | mostly | mostly | mostly | mostly | mostly |
| `delay` | no | no | no | no | no | no |
| Events | no | no | no | no | no | no |
| Exponentiation spelling | `^` | `pow()` | `^` | `^` | `^` | `SIMINT_POWER` |

"mostly" for an assignment-rule compartment means the dilution term is formed
whenever the rule can be differentiated; see below.

# Algebraic rules

An algebraic rule is a constraint `0 = f(...)`, not a derivative. SBML does not
say which variable a given rule determines, so `r2sbml` works it out.

## Rules linear in one unknown become assignments

An *unknown* is a species, parameter or compartment that is not constant and
has no rate or assignment rule. When a rule names exactly one unknown and is
linear in it, `r2sbml` solves it, and the rule becomes an ordinary assignment
rule — which every target supports. Here `0 = k - 0.9` defines a parameter that
has no value of its own:

```{r algebraic-linear}
linear <- sbml_file('
<listOfParameters><parameter id="k" constant="false"/></listOfParameters>
<listOfRules><algebraicRule><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
<apply><minus/><ci>k</ci><cn>0.9</cn></apply></math></algebraicRule></listOfRules>')
out <- convert(linear, "mrgsolve")
grep("k = ", readLines(out), value = TRUE)
```

The solution is `x = -f(0) / (f(1) - f(0))`, written out as is rather than
simplified, which is why it reads as it does. Solving repeats until nothing
more can be solved, so a rule that becomes linear
in one unknown once another has been solved is solved too. Every algebraic rule
in the SBML Test Suite is of this kind.

The solution divides by the unknown's coefficient. A rule such as
`(k3 + 1) * S = T` with `k3 = -1` determines nothing, and the generated code
returns `NaN` there.

## Coupled or nonlinear rules become a DAE where the target can solve one

What is left — rules that each name several unknowns, or are nonlinear in the
one they name — makes the model a differential-algebraic system. deSolve,
MATLAB and Julia can each solve one, and `r2sbml` emits a real DAE for them: a
`daspk` residual function, or a singular mass matrix. `sbmlalgebraicrules.xml`
is such a model, since both of its rules name both `E` and `ES`. The constraint
is genuinely enforced:

```{r dae-works, eval = has_desolve}
out <- convert(ex("sbmlalgebraicrules.xml"))
env <- new.env(); source(out, local = env)
d <- as.data.frame(deSolve::daspk(y = env$InitialAmounts, dy = env$InitialDerivatives,
                                  times = seq(0, 10, by = 2), res = env$massBalances,
                                  parms = env$parameters))
max(abs(d$E + d$ES - d$E_total))    # constraint residual, ~1e-13
```

mrgsolve, rxode2 and ubiquity integrate ODEs only. There the rule is written out
as a comment, the species it constrains is left at a zero derivative, and a
warning is raised:

```{r dae-warns}
convert(ex("sbmlalgebraicrules.xml"), "mrgsolve")
```

## The DAE path has three further limits

**The system must be square.** Only species are candidates for a DAE row, and a
DAE is emitted only when the number of remaining algebraic rules equals the
number of undetermined species. Otherwise `r2sbml` falls back to comments and a
warning rather than guess. A bipartite matching over the variables each rule
names would widen this; it is not implemented.

**Consistent initial conditions are assumed, not checked.** A DAE has to start
on the constraint manifold. `sbmlalgebraicrules.xml` happens to. A model that
does not will fail inside the solver — `daspk` cannot find consistent initial
conditions, `ode15s` rejects the initial state — and **the error will not
mention SBML or `r2sbml`**.

**`daspk`'s `estini` cannot be used as is.** It can estimate consistent initial
values, but requires the algebraic equations to come last in the residual
vector, which the current row ordering does not guarantee.

# Compartments whose volume changes

When a volume changes, so does every concentration in it: `[S] = n/V` gives the
dilution term `-[S] * (dV/dt) / V`, which libSBML's own reaction conversion
leaves out and `r2sbml` adds.

A compartment with a **rate rule** is fully handled: `dV/dt` is the rule.

A compartment with an **assignment rule** `V = g(...)` needs `dV/dt` worked out
by differentiating `g` — with respect to time, and through the chain rule with
respect to every integrated state it reads. `r2sbml` does that for sums,
products, quotients, powers and roots, `exp`, `ln`, `log`, and the
trigonometric and hyperbolic functions:

```{r volume-rule}
volume <- function(rule) sbml_file(sprintf('
<listOfCompartments><compartment id="c" size="1" constant="false"/></listOfCompartments>
<listOfSpecies><species id="A" compartment="c" initialConcentration="2"
  hasOnlySubstanceUnits="false" boundaryCondition="false" constant="false"/></listOfSpecies>
<listOfParameters><parameter id="g" value="1" constant="true"/></listOfParameters>
<listOfRules><assignmentRule variable="c">
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">%s</math></assignmentRule></listOfRules>', rule))
time <- '<csymbol encoding="text" definitionURL="http://www.sbml.org/sbml/symbols/time">time</csymbol>'

growing <- volume(sprintf('<apply><plus/><cn>1</cn><apply><times/><ci>g</ci>%s</apply></apply>', time))
out <- convert(growing)
grep("dA_dt = ", readLines(out), value = TRUE)    # V = 1 + g t, so dV/dt = g
```

It falls back to a warning, and no dilution term, when the rule reads a species
(whose own derivative would then depend on the volume's), or depends through
time or a state on `piecewise`, `min`, `max`, `abs`, the inverse trigonometric
functions or `factorial`:

```{r volume-rule-warns}
capped <- volume(sprintf('<apply><min/><cn>5</cn><apply><plus/><cn>1</cn>
  <apply><times/><ci>g</ci>%s</apply></apply></apply>', time))
convert(capped)
```

Events that change a compartment size are not handled, for the same reason
events in general are not.

# `delay`

SBML's `delay` csymbol passes through unchanged into every target:

```{r delay}
out <- convert(ex("sbmldelay.xml"))
grep("delay", readLines(out), value = TRUE)
```

`delay()` is not a function in base R, in C++, in MATLAB or in Julia, so this
code does not run anywhere. A delay-differential equation needs a different
solver interface entirely — `deSolve::lagvalue()` for R, and the equivalent per
target. Only the ubiquity writer notices:

```{r delay-ubiquity}
convert(ex("sbmldelay.xml"), "ubiquity")
```

For the other five targets this is **silent**. `sbmldelay.xml` is the one
example model whose generated deSolve, mrgsolve, rxode2, MATLAB and Julia output
will not run.

# Events

Events are not exported at all. They survive as a number in the header comment
and nothing else:

```{r events}
out <- convert(ex("sbmlevent.xml"))
grep("events", readLines(out), value = TRUE)
```

`sbmlevent.xml` has two events, and neither appears in the generated code. The
simulation will run — and will silently ignore every trigger, delay and event
assignment in the model. You can still inspect them from R:

```{r events-inspect}
getEventMath(getModel(ex("sbmlevent.xml")))
```

Translating them would mean mapping SBML triggers onto each target's own
mechanism — deSolve's `events`/`roots`, mrgsolve's `$EVENT`, and so on — which
differ enough that there is no shared representation to generate from.

# Mathematics

Most of SBML's MathML is rewritten into each target's own spelling: `piecewise`
becomes nested conditionals, `ceiling`, infinity, `NaN` and the booleans are
spelled per target, and the Level 3 Version 2 functions (`sec` and its
relatives, the inverse functions, `quotient`, `rem`, `implies`, `exponentiale`,
`avogadro`, `log` with a base, `root`, and n-ary relationals and logical
operators) are expanded into functions every target has. A logarithm with a
base and a cube root, for instance:

```{r maths}
maths <- sbml_file('
<listOfParameters>
<parameter id="x" value="8" constant="true"/>
<parameter id="a" constant="false"/><parameter id="b" constant="false"/>
</listOfParameters>
<listOfRules>
<assignmentRule variable="a"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
<apply><log/><logbase><cn>2</cn></logbase><ci>x</ci></apply></math></assignmentRule>
<assignmentRule variable="b"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
<apply><root/><degree><cn>3</cn></degree><ci>x</ci></apply></math></assignmentRule>
</listOfRules>')
out <- convert(maths)
grep("^ +[ab] = ", readLines(out), value = TRUE)
out <- convert(maths, "mrgsolve")
grep("^double [ab] = ", readLines(out), value = TRUE)
```

The cube root is longer than `x^(1/3)` because it keeps the sign of `x`: an odd
root of a negative number is real, but `x^(1/3)` is `NaN` there. The mrgsolve
spelling shows one more rewrite: every whole-number literal is written as a
double, because in C++ `1 / 3` divides as integers and is 0. The ubiquity
output does the same, since ubiquity compiles it as C.

What is not covered:

**`root(n, x)`** is written `x^(1/n)`, except that for a literal odd `n` it
keeps the sign of `x`, so the cube root of `-8` is `-2`. A degree that is not a
literal number cannot be checked for oddness, so there a negative `x` gives
`NaN` even when a real root exists.

**`factorial`** passes through unchanged. It is a function in R and MATLAB; in
C++ and Julia it is untested, and Julia's `factorial` accepts only an integer.

**`quotient` and `rem`** follow libSBML's own definitions, `floor(a/b)` and
`a - b * floor(a/b)`. No test case has a negative operand, so whether that
matches the intended truncation towards zero is unchecked.

**ubiquity** has no spelling for `factorial`, `delay`, `or`, `not` or `xor`. They are written out as plain calls, and the writer puts a `# WARNING`
block in the file as well as raising an R warning. That matters more for
ubiquity than elsewhere: `build_system()` accepts the file, and the failure
surfaces much later as a C compile error naming a shared object, with nothing
pointing back at the model.

**Initial assignments are evaluated by libSBML**, which treats a numeric
`piecewise` condition other than 0 or 1 as false. A model relying on
`piecewise(0, 5, 1)` taking the first branch gets the second.

# Values and names

## Values the model leaves undefined

SBML lets a parameter omit its value and a compartment its size, as long as
something else defines it. When nothing does, `r2sbml` writes the target's
not-a-number and warns, naming the variable, rather than make up a plausible
value:

```{r undefined}
undefined <- sbml_file('
<listOfParameters><parameter id="k" constant="true"/></listOfParameters>')
convert(undefined)
```

The same warning appears for a `NaN` the model assigns deliberately, where it
is less apt.

## Ids the target reserves

An SBML id can be a reserved word in the target (`TRUE`, `Inf`, `if`), a
built-in constant, or a name the generated code itself uses (`time`, Julia's
`p`, MATLAB's `t` and `y`). Such an id is renamed by appending `_`, and the
conversion says so:

```{r reserved}
reserved <- sbml_file('
<listOfParameters><parameter id="Inf" value="2" constant="true"/>
<parameter id="v" constant="false"/></listOfParameters>
<listOfRules><assignmentRule variable="v"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
<apply><times/><ci>Inf</ci><cn>3</cn></apply></math></assignmentRule></listOfRules>')
out <- tempfile()
msg <- capture.output(convertReactions(reserved, out, format = "Julia"))
grep("Renamed", msg, value = TRUE)
```

deSolve output keeps the SBML id as every name its results carry, so its
columns are unchanged — except for a renamed compartment, which is a top-level
variable there. The other targets show the new name. Three gaps remain:

- rxode2 exports no list of its reserved names, so `r2sbml`'s list holds only
  those found by probing it.
- An id that is not a valid name in the target at all, rather than a reserved
  one, is not renamed. libSBML promotes a local parameter `k1` of reaction
  `_J0` to `_J0_k1`, which R does not accept.
- rxode2's `ini()` block rejects an infinite parameter value, and no spelling
  avoids that.

# No validation is performed

`getModel()` and `convertReactions()` stop if libSBML reports an error while
*reading* the file, but reading is not validation. Neither runs a consistency
check, so a model that loads cleanly may still be semantically invalid —
inconsistent units, an overdetermined system, a species referenced before it is
defined.

If you need validation, run it through libSBML's own validator or the
[online SBML validator](https://sbml.org/facilities/validator/) first. `r2sbml` assumes
the model it is given is a correct one.

# Quirks of the query functions

These are not code-generation issues; they affect the inspection API.

## Initial values are reported as the file states them

`getSpeciesIC()` returns whichever of `initialAmount` or `initialConcentration`
the model actually sets — a species carries one or the other, never both — and
names the result by species id:

```{r species-ic}
model <- getModel(ex("sbmlsimple.xml"))
getSpeciesIC(model)
```

**No unit conversion is applied.** That is deliberate: a query function should
report the file. So a model that mixes amount-valued and concentration-valued
species yields a vector that mixes units, and `getSpeciesIC()` deliberately
disagrees with the initial conditions `convertReactions()` writes, which are
divided by compartment volume because the generated ODE integrates
concentrations:

```{r species-ic-vs-converted}
out <- convert(ex("sbmlsimple.xml"))
grep("^ +E = [0-9]", readLines(out), value = TRUE)   # 5e-07 = 5e-21 / 1e-14
```

`getSpeciesTable()` shows which column each species used, so you can tell the
units apart:

```{r species-table}
getSpeciesTable(model)[, c("ID", "InitialConcentration", "InitialAmount")]
```

A species that sets neither attribute — its value comes from an initial
assignment or a rule — is reported as `NA` rather than a fabricated `0`. Note
that `NA` there is distinct from the `NaN` in the table above, which marks the
attribute the model simply did not use.

## Names fall back to the id

SBML distinguishes `id`, which every element must have, from `name`, an
optional human label. `getSpeciesNames()` and `getCmtNames()` both return the
`name` where one is set and the `id` otherwise, which is how SBML tools
conventionally display an element:

```{r species-names}
getSpeciesNames(model)
getCmtNames(model)
```

None of the ten examples sets a `name`, so both come back as ids. Use
`getSpeciesTable()`, which keeps `ID` and `Name` in separate columns, if you
need to know whether a label was actually present.

## Absent components raise an error

```{r stopping, error = TRUE}
getRuleMath(model)     # sbmlsimple.xml has no rules
```

This is by design: a query for a component the model does not have is an error,
not a zero-row result. The message names the component, so a caller catching it
can tell "no rules" from "no parameters" without capturing stdout.

# Things that are correct but easy to misread

**`NaN` in `getSpeciesTable()` is not a bug.** It marks the attribute the model
did not set.

**Console output is not part of the return value.** `getRuleMath()` and friends
return `0` invisibly and print their content, so `x <- getRuleMath(m)` gives you
`0`. Use `capture.output()`.

**Compartment volumes are constants in the generated code** — when the model
says they are constant. That is not the volume being ignored.

**Assignment-rule variables appear as outputs, not states.** They are
recomputed from the states at every time point and returned beside them; the
solver never integrates them.

**ubiquity bounds are `-inf inf`.** Deliberate: an SBML value may be zero or
negative, and a lower bound above the value would be inconsistent. ubiquity
itself maps the `-inf` lower bound to `.Machine$double.xmin`, the smallest
*positive* double — harmless for simulation, wrong for parameter estimation.

**The generated header comment counts model components**, including ones that
were expanded away (function definitions, initial assignments) or not exported
(events). It describes the SBML file, not the generated code.

# Generated code is a starting point

Even where everything above is satisfied, treat the output as a first draft:

- The time span is a placeholder — `[0 10]` for MATLAB, `(0.0, 10.0)` for Julia,
  and nothing at all for the R targets, which leave the call to you.
- Solver tolerances are defaults, and no target's generated code sets them.
  Some models are stiff enough to need tuning: `sbmlmutlicompartment.xml` (rate
  constants from 2500 to 25000) integrates cleanly to `t = 1` with `deSolve`'s
  defaults but exhausts `lsoda`'s step budget before `t = 5`, returning early
  with a warning rather than an error.
- No unit checking is performed. `r2sbml` converts initial conditions between
  amount and concentration using compartment volume, but it does not verify that
  the model's declared units are mutually consistent, and it does not convert
  between, say, millilitres and litres.

# The SBML Test Suite cases that still fail

For completeness, the four in-scope cases that fail:

| Case | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| 01121 | `_J0_k1`, a promoted local parameter, is not a valid R name |
| 01282 | libSBML's evaluation of a numeric `piecewise` condition |
| 01323 | a relative error of about 3.5e-08, just outside the case's tolerance |
| 01486 | not yet diagnosed |

# Where these are tracked

The package keeps `todo.md` in its source repository recording each known gap
along with how it was found, so a claim here can be checked against the
reasoning behind it before anyone acts on it. The test suite covers every
limitation that has a defined behaviour — the warnings, the fallbacks, and the
closed-form solutions used to verify the DAE and dilution paths.
